article.headline: OpenAI's Symphony Lets the Ticket Queue Run the Agent
article.lede: OpenAI has open-sourced **Symphony**, a framework that connects a project-management backlog directly to autonomous coding agents. The design is deliberately plain: a scheduler pulls tickets, dispatches them to workers, and lets each worker run until the job is done. The result, with 18,000 GitHub stars, is attracting attention less for novelty than for restraint.
article.body:
Symphony's pitch is organisational as much as technical. Rather than asking engineers to hover over an AI pair-programmer, it asks them to write tickets in *Linear* — the project-management tool already used by many software teams — and then step back. A *cron job* (a scheduled process that fires on a fixed interval) polls Linear for open work, claims each ticket, and hands it to an isolated worker agent. The worker then runs autonomously until it either completes the task or gets stuck.

The architectural choice that the poster highlights as elegant is how state is persisted. Instead of a bespoke database or an in-memory object that evaporates if the process crashes, each worker uses a Linear *comment* on the ticket as its scratchpad — appending intermediate reasoning, partial results, and next steps in plain text. The comment thread becomes both the audit trail and the recovery point. If a worker dies mid-run, the next one can read the thread and pick up where the last left off.

The poster describes each worker as running a **Ralph loop**, a term specific to Symphony's internals that does not appear to have a standard industry definition based on the available sources. From context it refers to Symphony's core agent-execution cycle: the loop in which a worker reads its current state, takes an action, writes back to Linear, and repeats. The name may be an internal codename or a reference to a component in OpenAI's codebase; its etymology cannot be confirmed from the sources provided.

What makes the design notable is the absence of a custom orchestration layer. Symphony does not introduce a new protocol for agent communication or a proprietary state machine. It treats Linear — a tool teams already pay for and understand — as a durable queue, a state store, and a human-readable log simultaneously. The engineering taste on display is the refusal to build more than the problem requires.

The broader significance is as a reference architecture. As teams experiment with autonomous coding agents, Symphony offers a replicable pattern: use your existing issue tracker as the interface, use comments as cheap persistent memory, and use a cron job as the only scheduler you need. Whether that pattern holds at scale — or whether teams hit the limits the poster glosses over — remains an open question, though early community reaction is notably warmer than for more elaborate agent frameworks.

concepts.definition: A scheduled process in Unix-style systems that runs a command at fixed time intervals — every minute, every hour, or on any calendar pattern. In Symphony's case, the cron job is the only orchestrator: it wakes up, checks Linear for new tickets, and hands them to worker agents.

A project-management tool popular with software teams for tracking bugs, features, and tasks as structured tickets. Symphony uses Linear as both the input queue (tickets to be worked) and the state store (comments on those tickets), avoiding any purpose-built database.

Information that survives a process crash or restart because it is written to durable storage rather than held in memory. Symphony achieves this cheaply by writing agent progress directly into Linear comment threads, which are stored on Linear's servers.

The poster's term for Symphony's core agent-execution cycle, in which a worker reads its current state, performs an action, writes results back to Linear, and repeats. The name appears to be internal to Symphony's codebase; its precise etymology is not confirmed in the available sources.

A software process that accepts a programming task, breaks it into steps, writes and runs code, inspects results, and iterates — without a human directing each step. Symphony treats each Linear ticket as one complete task for one such agent.

repos.summary: Symphony is an open-source framework from OpenAI that turns Linear tickets into isolated, autonomous coding runs. A cron job dispatches tickets to worker agents; each worker uses a Linear comment thread as a persistent scratchpad and runs until the task is complete or it stalls. With 18,000 stars and 2,000 forks, it has become a reference architecture for teams that want agent-driven development without custom orchestration infrastructure.

article.fact_check: The poster's architectural description — cron job, Linear dispatch, comment-based state — is consistent with the repo's own summary and cannot be independently verified from the research sources (all three X.com pages were inaccessible due to JavaScript restrictions). The term 'Ralph loop' cannot be confirmed against external documentation; it may be an internal codename. No factual claims in the tweet appear demonstrably wrong, but the characterisation 'all you need' elides questions of scale, error handling, and context-window limits that more critical voices in the thread appear to raise.
